en: The Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Flower-Heap Pavilion Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Dispersing Grandee and Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
the Dharma-transmitting Master, the Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Blessed One was staying at Lake Anavatapta in the palace of the Naga King Anathapindada,
together with a great assembly of four hundred and fifty bhiksus.
Furthermore, there was an assembly of one thousand great bodhisattvas, such as the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍita,
all of whom had attained dhāraṇīs and were perfected in the ten stages (bhūmi).
Having received the empowerment, they occupy the stage of the successor to the Buddhas;
donning the great armor, they advance toward the virtues of all Buddhas;
their minds do not regress, and their fame is heard everywhere.
Such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as these all came from other directions and assembled there.
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Siṃhavikrīḍita...
Rising from his seat, he bared his right shoulder,
approached the World-Honored One, knelt with his right knee on the ground,
joined his palms in reverent solemnity, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān, how is the mass of merit of a Buddha to be obtained?
Furthermore, regarding those who make offerings to the Tathāgata,
how is it that their cause and fruit are immeasurable and boundless?"
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately grant me instruction.
Having spoken thus, he remained with his mind concentrated.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrīḍita, saying:
Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You have now asked me how the Tathāgata’s accumulation of merit is attained,
and also regarding those who make offerings to the Tathāgata.
"How is it that cause and effect are immeasurable and boundless?
Listen attentively, and I shall now explain this for you.
The Buddha said, "Good son,"
The Tathāgata possesses five dharmas that are endowed with immeasurable and boundless merit.
What are these five dharmas?
They are namely: ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
"Good son, the Tathāgata is fully endowed with these five dharmas and immeasurable merits;
therefore, he has attained an accumulation of merit that is infinite and boundless.
Good son, if one makes offerings to the Tathāgata..."
One shall attain nirvana; if those of the three vehicles, according to their respective aspirations, each perceive [the Buddha] as they do, they shall likewise attain nirvana.
Good son, if one perceives the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha...
With a pure mind, one should faithfully take refuge, revere, and praise [the Buddha],
and further provide offerings of all necessities, such as clothing, bedding,
and medicinal requisites for the sick.
The karmic rewards obtained will be immeasurable and boundless.
Son of good family, if, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa,
there should be those who obtain even as much as a mustard seed of the Tathāgata’s relics and offer them worship, [the merit shall likewise be immeasurable].
The karmic fruit obtained is supreme among all things.
Furthermore, one should perform various meritorious deeds;
if one makes offerings to the relics of the Tathāgata, [the merit is likewise unsurpassed].
That merit is supreme.
It is like the lion’s play.
Furthermore, suppose there were someone who held a mass of jewels as vast as Mount Sumeru.

The fruit and reward obtained from practicing giving and making offerings to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is not equal to that of a lay or ordained bodhisattva who resolves upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
He offered a single coin as a gift and offering to the Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
by virtue of those roots of goodness from his previous skillful means.
Compared to the roots of goodness of the subsequent skillful means,
it does not equal even one hundredth part,
nor does it equal even one thousandth part.
It does not approach even one part in a hundred thousand;
indeed, it cannot be reached by any calculation, fraction, number, analogy,
or even by the most subtle of analogies or mathematical reckoning.
Good son, furthermore, whether the Tathāgata remains in the world for a hundred years, a thousand years, or even a hundred thousand years,
once his manifestations and transformations are completed,
after his parinirvāṇa, a wondrous stūpa shall be erected with the Buddha’s relics.
Furthermore, if there is a person who, at the site of this stūpa,
coats the ground with fragrant mud to create a maṇḍala,
and provides offerings of flower garlands, unguents, incense, and lamps with a resolute mind;
Even if one offers a single flower or a single lamp as an act of worship;
or uses a broom or a whisk to sweep away dust and filth;
or takes a single handful of water to sprinkle for purification.
Such a person, by virtue of their sincere resolve, shall obtain immeasurable merit.
Although this person possessed sinful karma in previous lives that would have caused them to fall into the Avīci Hell,
because they made offerings at the stupa, [they are now liberated].
All karmic retributions from past lives will be completely extinguished.
Good son, if there should be another person who gives rise to even a single thought of taking refuge in the Buddha, [their transgressions shall likewise be eradicated].
Furthermore, they shall not regress nor be contemptuous.
Such persons, throughout the future— whether for a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, or even a hundred thousand kalpas—
will always experience superior merit and be born among humans and devas, never again falling into any of the evil realms.
"Good son, I now proclaim this Flower-Heap Pavilion Dhāraṇī Sūtra for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings in the heavens and among humans."
Good son, if there should be anyone who obtains this *Puṣpakūṭāgāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra*,
and with a sincere mind receives, maintains, recites, and makes offerings to it,
and furthermore explains its true meaning and intent extensively for others;
Such a person shall never fall into any of the evil realms,
nor be born into a lowly lineage;
they will always be reborn in the superior states of humans and devas.
With all faculties complete, they attain the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives;
they possess various kinds of profound eloquence and constantly encounter the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
Furthermore, they shall receive the Tathāgata’s mindful protection and attain a bodhicitta that never regresses.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this dhāraṇī, saying:
Tadyathā: dhāraṇi dhāraṇi, muñca praprasavari, siddhiñjanadri, natha jñinirhari, arugaya.
vati (2) buddhavati (3) vīryogate rāśubhagate (4) tejovati (5) viśālamati dharimāvāsini (6) akṣayyakṣarabuddhe (7) svāhā (8) || 10 ||
1. Kala-pa; 2. va-ti; 3. ā-mṛ-ta; 4. kala-pe; 5.
hu-ḍa-śā-ni; 6. te-jova-ti; 7. nitya-samādhi-te; 8. te-jova-ti; 9. ti-kṣaṇam.
*Hañjarya-mūde svāhā.* (16) "Good son, this dhāraṇī has been proclaimed together by the infinite and boundless Tathāgatas, the Buddhas of the ten directions."
Furthermore, if there should be anyone who hears the name of this *dhāraṇī* sūtra and,
with a heart of utmost sincerity, reverently believes in and makes offerings to it,
that person shall obtain immeasurable and boundless merit in the future.
Furthermore, if a person maintains this dhāraṇī and has accomplished the preliminary practices,
then during the second, third, or eighth month, they should...
Beginning on the eighth day of the waxing moon,
one should arouse a heart of utmost sincerity and, throughout a single day and night,
recite this dhāraṇī and keep the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in mind during the six periods.
With an undistracted mind,
one should further offer various kinds of offerings— such as scented ointments, exquisite flowers, burning incense, and lit lamps—
without interruption until the fifteenth day, at which time one will certainly behold the World-Honored One.
Seated upon the Lotus Treasury Throne, he expounds the dharma of dhāraṇīs.
Those who maintain and recite them shall, at that very time, obtain the fulfillment of their aspirations;
all mental defilements will be entirely removed, and they will realize the supernormal power of recollecting past lives.
They attain various meditative concentrations and abide in the Four Noble Truths;
they understand the meanings of all dharmas, as well as treatises and the arts and crafts;
even at the time of their death, their faculty of hearing does not fail.
They are able to discern all supreme matters;
even when they hear the Tathāgata preaching the untainted [teachings] such as the Four Noble Truths.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished speaking this dhāraṇī sūtra, [said:]
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrīḍita,
together with the assembly of great bodhisattvas and great bhikṣus,
as well as devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, they were all greatly rejoiced; they prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew.
This concludes the *Buddha-bhāṣita-puṣpasañcaya-kūṭāgāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
